blocks.source: Vol III, Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards, § Fallacies and Pitfalls
blocks.md: A rollout group can easily contain positive rewards without establishing a sound solution, and a policy update can fit that group without improving the deployed agent. The pitfalls detailed below each turn a narrow, scoped measurement into an unwarranted conclusion, and each carries a concrete systems cost.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Rollout loop sizing matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Agent RL throughput is set by the rollout loop, not the gradient step, so the serial slot cycle caps capacity and Amdahl's law bounds any single-stage speedup.

questions.q: The section **Fallacies and Pitfalls** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: GRPO replaces the learned critic with G rollouts per task and broadcasts one standardized coefficient to every sampled token of a rollout, and its clipping and KL estimator choices change how that signal is weighted.
A terminal reward gives every turn the same reward-to-go, so separating a useful step from a faulty one is bought with a critic, more samples, or step-level signals, each at its own cost.
Agent RL throughput is set by the rollout loop, not the gradient step, so the serial slot cycle caps capacity and Amdahl's law bounds any single-stage speedup.
RLVR scores sampled rollouts with a programmatic check, so the update learns only what the sampler reaches and the reward distinguishes, and a task the policy never solves gives zero signal.
